name: Fat grafting for facial asymmetry

lead: Fat grafting harvests a patient's own fat, usually by liposuction, processes it and injects it into areas lacking volume. For asymmetry, the payoff is a visibly fuller, more even face once the thinner side is built up to match.

The fat is washed or filtered and re-injected into the target area. Facial fat grafting is widely used in reconstructive and cosmetic surgery. A systematic review reports that a main drawback is high and unpredictable absorption, so surgeons judge retention from experience; the studies reviewed concern facial volume restoration in general rather than asymmetry specifically.

paras: It is done by a surgeon, often under sedation or anaesthesia, with fat taken from areas such as the abdomen or thighs. Swelling settles over weeks and the final volume shows after some of the graft is absorbed. Because retention varies, some patients have repeat sessions.

Reported problems include swelling, bruising, contour irregularities, infection, fat necrosis and reabsorption; a systematic review asks whether facial fat grafting is worth its risk. Results may need touch-ups.

angle.text: Surgeons move a patient's own fat into the thinner side of the face so the two sides match in volume, giving a visibly fuller, more balanced face. Fat transfer is a standard reconstructive and aesthetic technique, with graft survival varying between patients.

lead: Fat grafting, also called fat transfer or lipofilling, moves a person's own fat from one body area to another in three stages: harvesting, usually by liposuction, processing, and reinjection.[1] For facial asymmetry, surgeons use it to add volume to the leaner or flatter side of the face so that the two sides match more closely.[2][3]

The appeal is direct: because the filler is the patient's own tissue, it is described as biocompatible, and it can be placed in cheeks, temples, jawline, chin, under-eye hollows and other areas where one side looks deflated.[1][4] Looksmaxxing discussions often cite it alongside synthetic fillers and implants as a way to even out volume or build contour without a foreign material.

Research on facial fat grafting is substantial but mostly concerns volume restoration and rejuvenation in general rather than asymmetry specifically. A systematic review and meta-analysis found that the main drawback is high and variable absorption of the grafted fat, so retention has often been judged by surgeon experience.[5]

Reviews place the technique's origin in 1893, with a long period of limited acceptance before it became popular among plastic surgeons in recent decades, helped by the ease of harvesting fat with little donor-site morbidity.[3]
infobox: Cheeks, temples, under-eye, jaw, chin, nasolabial area[2][13]
Congenital, post-traumatic, post-surgical and age-related causes[3][11]

paras: Fat is typically harvested with liposuction from the abdomen, flanks or thighs, then washed, filtered or centrifuged, and injected in small aliquots through fine cannulas at several depths.[1][6] Soft-tissue volume loss is regarded as a key component of facial aging, and fat is used alongside fillers to replace it.[4] The procedure can be done under local or general anaesthesia.[1]

Surgeons distinguish grafts by particle size. Macrofat is used for volume, microfat for finer contouring, and nanofat, which is emulsified and contains few intact adipocytes, is used for skin quality; reviews describe where each is used.[7][8] Adipose-derived stem cells are credited in part for the regenerative effects reported with fat grafting, and trials of stem-cell enriched grafts are registered.[1][9]

Wikipedia's article on fat grafting describes the procedure as moving a person's own fat to fill irregularities or depressions, in three stages of harvesting, processing and reinjection, under local or general anaesthesia. It also describes newer stem-cell-enriched techniques and so-called nanografts, which contain no intact fat cells but are said to retain stem-cell content, and notes uses beyond the face such as breast reconstruction, the Brazilian butt lift, the back of the hands, correction of a low nasal dorsum, and scars.[1]

Everyday faces are never perfectly symmetric. Wikipedia's description of facial symmetry separates fluctuating asymmetry, small random left-right differences measured against the midline, from directional asymmetry, a consistent bias across people; the eyes, nose and mouth sit on average slightly left of the axis through the ears, a difference of about 2 degrees at birth that falls to about 0.5 degrees in adults.[10] Normal variation of this kind is the background against which surgeons judge whether one side of the face is visibly deficient.

Larger differences can come from congenital conditions such as hemifacial microsomia, a birth condition affecting mainly the ears, mouth and jaw, usually on one side, with an estimated incidence of about 1 in 3,500 to 4,500 births; its treatment typically centres on the jaw, using distraction osteogenesis or rib grafts, with surgery often delayed because facial growth changes the picture.[11] Asymmetry can also follow trauma, tumour surgery, or ageing, when volume loss is uneven.[3] Fat grafting is generally discussed as a soft-tissue option that sits beside bony procedures rather than replacing them.[3][12]

sections.h: How people use it to look more balanced
paras: The appearance logic runs in a short chain: fat is taken from an area where it is plentiful, a leaner or flatter facial zone receives it, and the added volume reduces the visible step between the two sides. Zones named in the surgical literature include the cheek, temple, jawline, chin, under-eye hollow and nasolabial area.[2][13] Because the material is the patient's own tissue, reviews describe it as biocompatible and as usable in places where a synthetic implant or filler is less suited.[1][4]

Researchers who rate faces report that symmetry is one of several features, alongside averageness and youthfulness, associated with higher attractiveness ratings, and Wikipedia notes that effects were reported as larger for female faces in some studies.[10] Patients and surgeons describe the goal as balance rather than mathematical identity, because a face with perfectly mirrored halves is not the norm.[13][14]

Facial asymmetry can arise from developmental conditions, trauma, surgery or aging, and sometimes has no identified cause. Fat grafting is one of several tools, together with implants, fillers, and bony surgery. Published series describe full-face fat transfer combined with rhinoplasty to improve facial balance in Asian patients, and registered trials have examined structural fat grafting in craniofacial trauma.[12][15]
Reviews of injection volumes by facial subunit and of the lift-and-fill approach describe how surgeons distribute fat across fat compartments of the face.[13][14]

A review of soft-tissue contour deficiencies lists aesthetic, congenital and post-traumatic asymmetries, post-tumor defects and chronic wound sequelae among the reasons fat grafting is used for reconstruction.[3] In practice, surgeons describe judging how much volume each side of the face needs, adding fat on the flatter side and sometimes treating both sides, with the aim of balance rather than identical volume.[13][14]

A review of facial fat transfer describes an evolution from simple grafting to smaller-lobule microfat and adipose-derived stem cell nanofat injection, developed to address early limitations and the growing understanding that volume loss contributes to aging.[7] Harvesting technique has itself been a topic of study, with reviews comparing methods for obtaining fat for facial transfer.[6]

Wikipedia notes that the graft should not be manipulated too much and should be reinjected quickly to improve survival, and that micro-injection is used around the mouth and fat is used in the periorbital area including the lower eyelid.[1] Reviews report that adipose tissue contains more multipotent cells per gram than bone marrow, which is part of why regenerative claims are made about fat transfer.[3]

A study of rhinoplasty combined with full-face fat transfer in 20 Asian patients, followed for an average of 10.2 months, reported significant changes in nasal length and projection and a nasolabial angle that moved from a median of 106 to 101 degrees, along with three-dimensional evidence of changed facial volume and patient and surgeon satisfaction measures.[12] Fat is also used alongside fillers, implants and bone surgery in planning, with fillers and fat both aimed at replacing volume lost with age.[4]

The Aesthetic Plastic Surgery systematic review of volume retention found considerable variation between studies and noted that surgeons have largely relied on their own experience in judging how much to inject.[5] Reviews describe the search for predictable results as a long-standing theme of facial fat grafting.[16] Trials have compared processing methods, including filtered and washed versus centrifuged fat, and a randomized trial used three-dimensional volumetric analysis to compare three processing techniques.[17][18] Wikipedia notes that the body may reabsorb up to half of grafted fat in breast augmentation and that weight change can affect results.[1]

The meta-analysis of volume retention states that autologous fat grafting is common in facial reconstructive and cosmetic surgery and that the most important drawbacks are a high absorption rate and unpredictable retention, which is why surgeons rely on experience when deciding how much to inject.[5] A 25-patient prospective double-blind study compared filtered and washed fat with centrifuged fat, one of several efforts to find the best processing method.[17] A review of long-term sequelae describes concerns about perceived absorption of transplanted fat and about lumps and bulges around the eyes, alongside derivative benefits such as skin texture improvement and continued improvement in the grafted area over months to years.[19]

Reported complications include swelling, bruising, hematoma, altered sensation, hypertrophic scarring, infection, contour irregularities, fat necrosis, and reabsorption.[1] A 2022 systematic review of complications of facial fat grafting appraised the literature on risk, and an earlier review described limitations and long-term sequelae of fat transfer.[20][19]

Human research on facial fat grafting includes a systematic review and meta-analysis of volume retention, a 25-patient double-blind comparison of fat-processing methods, a randomized trial with three-dimensional volumetric analysis, a case series of rhinoplasty with full-face fat transfer in 20 patients, and systematic reviews of complications.[5][17][18][12][20]

No studies found specifically on fat grafting for cosmetic facial asymmetry framed as a looksmaxxing goal; the published work concerns facial volume restoration, reconstruction after trauma or tumor and rejuvenation.[3][15]

Registered trials listed on ClinicalTrials.gov include structural fat grafting after craniofacial trauma, a 26-person study of autologous facial fat grafting and skin texture and pigmentation, a pilot of fat grafting for facial acne scars, a study of contour deformities with hyperpigmentation, a trial of ultrasound-assessed macrofat retention after facelift, and a phase 1 trial of preconditioned adipose-derived stem cells in conditions such as Romberg disease and craniofacial microsomia.[21][22][23][24][25][9][15]

The International Society of Aesthetic Plastic Surgery's 14-year trend analysis tracks surgical and nonsurgical aesthetic procedures worldwide, including fat grafting among facial procedures.[26] Wikipedia describes facial rejuvenation as now emphasizing volume restoration with fat grafting and not only removal of skin.[1]

Facial fat grafting is performed by plastic and facial plastic surgeons and is usually described in professional literature as part of a wider toolkit that includes hyaluronic acid fillers, implants, lifts and bone contouring.[4][26] The ISAPS trend analysis covers procedure volumes worldwide, and reviews of facial rejuvenation describe a shift towards volume restoration rather than skin removal alone.[1][26]

On looksmax.org, threads discuss under-eye and nasolabial hollows and products marketed as topical lipofilling agents, with users asking how to apply them and whether they work for tear troughs.[27] Surgical fat transfer is mentioned in the same conversations as an alternative to hyaluronic acid fillers.
